prompt.context: A major auto service chain, Wheeler Dealer, has enjoyed healthy returns on its 30-store operation for the past 10 years. However, management feels that the chain needs to expand, as the current geographical areas in which they are based have become saturated. For the past couple of years, they have aggressively pursued a growth strategy, opening an additional 15 stores. However, it seems that this approach has had negative returns. For the first time in over a decade, the chain's profits dropped into the negative zone.
prompt.question: You were hired to figure out why the expansion has led to negative profits.

clarifying_info.q: What type of services has Wheeler Dealer traditionally provided?
clarifying_info.a: There are two main businesses under each roof: off-the-shelf car parts and garage mechanical services.

clarifying_info.q: Are these services provided in the newly developed chains as well?
Have competitors entered the market stealing market share?
clarifying_info.a: A few competitors have entered the market, but not too many. The expansion was planned to explore new markets and prevent the competition from growing.

clarifying_info.q: Have prices changed to help defray some of the costs associated with growth?
clarifying_info.a: No, prices have stayed the same.

clarifying_info.q: Do the two types of businesses (parts vs. garage service) have the same profit margin?
clarifying_info.a: No. The garage services cost the business a great deal more and the mechanics are very well trained, so they charge a premium. Profit margin on servicing cars is twice the profit margin of off-the-shelf products.

clarifying_info.q: Are the customers the same for both businesses?
clarifying_info.a: No. The customer that uses the garage service tends to come from a mid-to-high income bracket. Those that use the off-the-shelf auto parts tend to be of the lower-income bracket — they fix their cars on their own.

clarifying_info.q: Where has Wheeler Dealer traditionally been located?
clarifying_info.a: Mostly in, or very close to, the suburbs.

clarifying_info.q: Has the geographical location changed as they expanded?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. They saw certain urban areas as very inexpensive and located more in inner cities where there are a lot of used car sales.

framework: Understand the nature of the business: two revenue streams — off-the-shelf car parts (retail) and garage mechanical services
Analyze customer segmentation: suburban mid-to-high income customers use garage service; lower-income urban customers use parts retail
Compare profit margins: garage service margin is 2x the margin on off-the-shelf products
Assess geographic shift: original 30 stores in suburbs; new 15 stores in urban/inner-city areas
Identify revenue mix impact: inner-city locations attract parts-retail customers, not garage-service customers, degrading overall margin

questions.prompt: What is the root cause of the profitability decline?
questions.guidance: The candidate should connect the geographic expansion into inner cities with a customer mix shift. The new stores attract lower-income urban customers who buy off-the-shelf parts but do not use the higher-margin garage service. Since garage service margin is twice that of parts retail, displacing that revenue with lower-margin parts sales erodes overall profitability. Prices have not changed, and competition is not the primary driver.

questions.prompt: Why is price sensitivity a barrier to fixing the problem through price increases?
questions.guidance: Inner-city / lower-income customers are more price-sensitive. Raising prices on off-the-shelf parts in these locations risks volume loss without the margin boost that premium garage customers in the suburbs would absorb. The candidate should note that price is not a viable lever here.

brainstorming.prompt: What options does Wheeler Dealer have to return to profitability?

categories.name: Geographic retrenchment
ideas: Scale back from urban locations that cannot support garage-service demand
Re-focus new-store openings on suburban or peri-urban areas with mid-to-high income demographics

categories.name: Store-format optimization
ideas: Drop the garage service offering in under-performing inner-city stores to reduce costs
Convert under-performing stores to parts-only retail format with lower cost structure

categories.name: Revenue mix improvement
ideas: Market garage services more aggressively in locations where the suburban customer base exists
Introduce loyalty or maintenance packages targeted at higher-income customers

categories.name: Cost management
ideas: Reduce mechanic headcount at stores where garage utilization is low
Renegotiate leases or exit high-cost inner-city sites

categories.name: Competitive positioning
ideas: Use the suburban stores as defensive barriers against new entrants
Partner with used-car dealers in inner-city areas to drive parts volume at scale

recommendation: Scale back from urban/inner-city locations where the high-margin garage service cannot attract the target customer (suburban, mid-to-high income)
Prioritize new store openings in suburban areas where the full dual-revenue model (parts + garage service) can be executed at healthy margins
risks: Exiting urban leases may incur break costs
Competitors could fill vacated urban locations and build scale
Suburban markets may already be partially saturated given the original 30-store footprint
next_steps: Audit each of the 15 new stores by garage-service utilization and contribution margin
Identify which stores can be converted to parts-only format versus exited entirely
Develop site-selection criteria for future expansion emphasizing suburban demographics and income levels
